audit_status.source_base: Hebrew Ruth famine, migration to Moab, bereavement, return, Ruth's attachment, and Naomi's lament narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for judges-period setting, famine migration, Ephrathite identity, Moabite wives, compounded widowhood, Naomi's return counsel, Orpah's dignified departure, Ruth's attachment oath, Divine-name language, Naomi/Mara wordplay, Shaddai lament, and barley-harvest arrival.

verses.restored: In days when judges judged, there was famine in land. A man from Bethlehem of Judah went to sojourn in fields of Moab—he, his wife, and his two sons.

familiar.text: Now it came to pass in the days when the judges ruled, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Bethlehemjudah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.

verses.restored: Name of man was Elimelech, name of his wife Naomi, and names of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion—Ephrathites from Bethlehem of Judah. They came to fields of Moab and were there.

familiar.text: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehemjudah. And they came into the country of Moab, and continued there.

verses.restored: Elimelech, husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons.

familiar.text: And Elimelech Naomi’s husband died; and she was left, and her two sons.

verses.restored: They took for themselves Moabite women as wives. Name of one was Orpah, and name of second Ruth. They dwelt there about ten years.

familiar.text: And they took them wives of the women of Moab; the name of the one was Orpah, and the name of the other Ruth: and they dwelled there about ten years.

verses.restored: Both of them also died, Mahlon and Chilion, and the woman was left without her two children and without her husband.

familiar.text: And Mahlon and Chilion died also both of them; and the woman was left of her two sons and her husband.

verses.restored: She arose with her daughters-in-law to return from fields of Moab, because she had heard in field of Moab that YHWH had visited his people by giving them bread.

familiar.text: Then she arose with her daughters in law, that she might return from the country of Moab: for she had heard in the country of Moab how that the LORD had visited his people in giving them bread.

verses.restored: She went out from place where she had been, and her two daughters-in-law with her. They went on road to return to land of Judah.

familiar.text: Wherefore she went forth out of the place where she was, and her two daughters in law with her; and they went on the way to return unto the land of Judah.

verses.restored: Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, Go, return, each woman to house of her mother. May YHWH do covenant-kindness with you, as you have done with the dead and with me.

familiar.text: And Naomi said unto her two daughters in law, Go, return each to her mother’s house: the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me.

verses.restored: May YHWH grant you that you find rest, each woman in house of her husband. She kissed them, and they lifted their voices and wept.

verses.restored: They said to her, No, but with you we will return to your people.

familiar.text: And they said unto her, Surely we will return with thee unto thy people.

verses.restored: Naomi said, Return, my daughters. Why should you go with me? Are there yet sons in my womb who could become husbands for you?

familiar.text: And Naomi said, Turn again, my daughters: why will ye go with me? are there yet any more sons in my womb, that they may be your husbands?

verses.restored: Return, my daughters, go, because I am too old to belong to a husband. Even if I said, There is hope for me—even if tonight I belonged to a husband and also bore sons—

familiar.text: And they lifted up their voice, and wept again: and Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her.

familiar.text: And she said, Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law.

familiar.text: Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me.

verses.restored: The two of them went until they came to Bethlehem. When they came to Bethlehem, all the city stirred because of them, and the women said, Is this Naomi?

familiar.text: So they two went until they came to Bethlehem. And it came to pass, when they were come to Bethlehem, that all the city was moved about them, and they said, Is this Naomi?

familiar.text: And she said unto them, Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.

familiar.text: I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty: why then call ye me Naomi, seeing the LORD hath testified against me, and the Almighty hath afflicted me?

verses.restored: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, with her, who returned from fields of Moab. They came to Bethlehem at beginning of barley harvest.

familiar.text: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter in law, with her, which returned out of the country of Moab: and they came to Bethlehem in the beginning of barley harvest.

translation_notes: The opening famine makes migration a survival response. Elimelech's family are sojourners in Moab; migration does not make them disloyal, impure, or less worthy.
Ruth and Orpah are repeatedly identified as Moabite women, yet the narrative presents them as loyal family members. Their ethnicity may not be used for xenophobia or anti-intermarriage ideology.
Naomi blesses both daughters-in-law for covenant-kindness toward the dead and toward her. Orpah's return is not betrayal or failed faith; she accepts the future Naomi urges upon her.
Naomi's marriage-and-sons reasoning reflects patriarchal survival structures in which widows had limited economic security. It is not a timeless definition of women's purpose.

Ruth's words are an attachment oath to Naomi that includes people, land, burial, and Divine allegiance. They must not become a formula for coercive conversion, forced assimilation, or severing migrants from prior identity.
Naomi names her bitterness directly and interprets her suffering through YHWH and Shaddai. The narrator preserves her lament without declaring that bereavement proves Divine punishment.
'Empty' describes Naomi's grief and loss, not Ruth's lack of value. Ruth is physically beside her, and the narrative will challenge Naomi's perception of absolute emptiness.
The barley-harvest timing introduces material possibility but does not cancel grief. Recovery begins amid bereavement rather than replacing it.
safety_note: Do not shame migrants, widows, childless people, Moabites, Orpah, or Naomi's lament. Do not preach Ruth's attachment as coerced conversion, romantic self-erasure, or proof that loyalty requires abandoning all boundaries. Preserve grief, chosen kinship, economic vulnerability, and each woman's dignity.
